title: Earn Your Bread, Stay Family
overview: Paul closes the letter by asking for prayer, then tells the church how to handle members who have stopped working and are living off others.

parts.label: Pray for us (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Paul asks the believers in Thessalonica to pray that his message keeps spreading and is welcomed elsewhere, as it was with them. He also asks for protection from hostile people where he is writing, most likely the city of Corinth.

parts.label: God will hold you steady (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Paul turns from his own danger to assure them that God keeps his promises and will guard them from the evil one, meaning the devil. He prays they will be shaped by God's love and by Christ's endurance, which may mean the patience Christ showed or patient waiting for his return.

parts.label: We worked for our keep (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: Paul tells them to keep their distance from members who refuse to work and live off others. He reminds them that he worked night and day rather than accept support he had a right to, and had already taught that whoever is unwilling to work should not eat.

parts.label: Busy doing nothing (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: Some were not busy with their own work but were busy in everyone else's business, a play on words in the original language. Paul urges them to settle down and earn their own food, and urges everyone else not to grow tired of doing good.

parts.label: Distance without hostility (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Anyone who ignores these instructions should be noticeably avoided so they feel the weight of it and reconsider. Yet they are still family, to be warned honestly, not treated as an enemy.

parts.label: Peace and a signature (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Paul prays for peace in a church strained by this conflict, then writes the closing greeting in his own hand, since he usually dictated letters to a helper. This proved the letter was really his, which mattered because earlier in the letter he warns about messages falsely claiming to come from him.

disagreement: Interpreters differ on why some members had stopped working: many think they believed Jesus' return was so close that ordinary work no longer mattered, while others think they were simply depending on wealthier members as patrons, as was common in that society.
think: What do you think a community owes someone who could pull their weight but chooses not to, and what does it still owe them anyway?
